claim: cd59 RNA is expressed in OLCs and SCs at 3 dpf
source: Intrigued by this elevated expression of cd59 in developing myelinating glial cells, we verified that cd59 RNA was expressed in OLCs and SCs with chromogenic ISH (CISH) and fluorescent ISH (FISH) at 3 days post fertilization (dpf) (Figure 2A–C)
evidence: This is verified by CISH and FISH experiments shown in Figure 2A–C

claim: cd59 expression is largely confined to developing myelinating glial cells at 3 dpf beyond expression in the heart and pancreas
source: Beyond expression in the heart and pancreas, cd59 expression is largely confined to developing myelinating glial cells at this stage
evidence: This is an observation from the ISH experiments

claim: cd59:tagrfp labels OLs and SCs with myelin-like processes
source: With in vivo, confocal imaging, mosaic labeling with our cd59:tagrfp construct revealed labeling of OLs and SCs with myelin-like processes (Figure 2D), indicating that cd59 is expressed in mature myelinating glial cells
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo confocal imaging shown in Figure 2D

claim: cd59 is not expressed in sox10:megfp-positive NCCs at 24 hpf
source: At 24 hpf, using CISH and FISH, we did not observe cd59 expression in sox10:megfp-positive NCCs, though we did see it in the hypochord and floor plate of the spinal cord at this stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by CISH and FISH experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: cd59 is expressed in the hypochord and floor plate of the spinal cord at 24 hpf
source: At 24 hpf, using CISH and FISH, we did not observe cd59 expression in sox10:megfp-positive NCCs, though we did see it in the hypochord and floor plate of the spinal cord at this stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by CISH and FISH experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: cd59 is sporadically expressed in sox10:megfp-positive cells along the pLLN at 36 and 48 hpf
source: At 36 and 48 hpf, when NCCs begin to develop into SCPs and iSCs, we detected sporadic expression of cd59 with FISH in sox10:megfp-positive cells along the posterior lateral line nerve (pLLN) in the PNS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D)
evidence: This is demonstrated by FISH experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D

claim: cd59 is robustly expressed within sox10:megfp-positive SCs along the pLLN at 72 hpf
source: By 72 hpf, we observed robust cd59 expression within sox10:megfp-positive SCs along the pLLN (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D)
evidence: This is demonstrated by FISH experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D

claim: SCs associated with spinal motor nerves do not express cd59
source: From our ISH data, we noticed that cd59 was not expressed in every SC. Notably, SCs associated with spinal motor nerves did not express cd59 (Figure 2A–C)

claim: cd59 expression is largely confined to SCs along the pLLN
source: Rather, cd59 expression was largely confined to SCs along the pLLN (Figure 2A–C)
evidence: This is an observation from ISH data shown in Figure 2A–C

claim: cd59:tagrfp-positive SCs express sox10, erbb3b, and mbp
source: To verify that cd59:tagrfp-positive SCs expressed canonical SC markers, including SRY-box transcription factor 10 (sox10), erb-b2 receptor tyrosine kinase 3b (erbb3b), and myelin basic protein a (mbpa), we examined pLLN SCs in transgenic and gene trap larvae co-expressing these markers with in vivo confocal imaging. As expected, cd59:tagrfp expression was observed in sox10, erbb3b, and mbp-positive SCs at 72 and 7 dpf (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–E), confirming that cd59:tagrfp-positive SCs express other known SC genes
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo confocal imaging shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–E

claim: cd59:tagrfp is only expressed in a subset of pLLN SCs (average of 4.4 ± 1.5% to 9.4 ± 3.8%)
source: Strikingly, when looking at SCs from 3 to 7 dpf, cd59:tagrfp was only expressed in a subset of pLLN SCs (average of 4.4 ± 1.5% to 9.4 ± 3.8% of pLLN SCs; Figure 2E and F)
evidence: This is quantitative data from immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 2E and F

claim: cd59 expression is only expressed in a subset of OLs

source: and was completely lacking in MEP glia

claim: cd59uva48 mutant has a 15 bp deletion at the splice site between exon 2 and intron 2
source: Targeting the end of the first coding exon (exon 2; Figure 3A), we recovered an allele with a 15 bp deletion that occurred across the exon 2–intron 2 splice site, generating a splice mutation (herein referred to as mutant cd59uva48; Figure 3B)
evidence: This is the characterization of the mutant allele generated in the study, shown in Figure 3A and B

claim: cd59uva48 mutant transcripts produce multiple splice variants with early stop codons
source: RT-PCR and Sanger sequencing analysis of mutant cd59uva48 transcripts revealed that multiple splice variants were produced compared to wildtype cd59, which produced a single transcript (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and E). Analysis of the mutant transcripts indicated that an early stop codon was generated in the N-terminal signal sequence, producing a severely truncated protein (10–48 AA compared to the 119 AA wildtype protein; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and G)
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-PCR and Sanger sequencing shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and E

claim: cd59uva48 mutant protein lacks the Ly6/uPAR domain and GPI-anchor signal sequence
source: Furthermore, the predicted proteins lacked the Ly6/uPAR domain and GPI-anchor signal sequence (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and G)
evidence: This is predicted from sequence analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and G

claim: The mutant Cd59 protein in cd59uva48 is expected to be nonfunctional
source: Therefore, the mutant Cd59 protein was expected to be nonfunctional
evidence: This is an inference based on the truncation and loss of functional domains

claim: cd59uva47 mutant has a 6 bp deletion near the end of exon 2
source: We also recovered an additional cd59 mutant allele, cd59uva47, which was produced with the same single-guide RNA (sgRNA). This mutant had a 6 bp deletion near the end of exon 2 that did not affect the splice site (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and D)
evidence: This is the characterization of the mutant allele generated in the study, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and D

claim: cd59uva47 mutant produces a single mutant transcript
source: and therefore produced a single mutant transcript (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-PCR shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: cd59uva47 mutant protein is missing two amino acids in the N-terminal signal sequence
source: Sequencing of the mutant cd59uva47 transcript predicted the absence of two amino acids (AA) in the N-terminal signal sequence, which would yield a slightly smaller protein (117 AA) compared to wildtype Cd59 (119 AA; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and G)
evidence: This is predicted from sequence analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and G

claim: cd59uva48 and cd59uva47 homozygous adults are viable and produce embryos with no anatomical, behavioral, or reproductive defects
source: Both cd59uva48 and cd59uva47 homozygous adults were viable and produced embryos with no anatomical, behavioral, or reproductive defects (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is an observation from the characterization of the mutant lines shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: Wildtype and mutant cd59uva48 larvae have sox10, mbp, and krox20-positive SCs along the pLLN at 72 hpf
source: Using CISH, we labeled wildtype and mutant cd59uva48 larvae with RNA probes against sox10, krox20 (also known as early growth response 2b or egr2b), and mbp at 72 hpf. Both wildtype and mutant larvae had sox10, mbp, and krox20-positive SCs along the pLLN (Figure 3E–G), indicating that Cd59 was not necessary for SC genesis or expression of genes necessary for SC maturation and myelination
evidence: This is demonstrated by CISH experiments shown in Figure 3E–G

claim: Cd59 is not necessary for SC genesis or expression of genes necessary for SC maturation and myelination
source: indicating that Cd59 was not necessary for SC genesis or expression of genes necessary for SC maturation and myelination
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the CISH data

claim: cd59 expression is significantly reduced in mutant cd59uva48 SCs compared to wildtype SCs

claim: cd59uva48 mutant RNA undergoes nonsense-mediated decay
source: indicating that cd59uva48 mutant RNA was being degraded through NMD and therefore could result in a loss of protein

claim: cd59uva48 mutants can be used as a loss-of-function model to study the role of Cd59 in developing SCs
source: However, our findings indicate that cd59uva48 mutants can be used as a loss-of-function model in which to study the role of Cd59 in developing SCs

claim: There are significantly more SCs in cd59uva48 mutant embryos and larvae compared to wildtype siblings at all stages from 36 hpf to 7 dpf

claim: cd59uva47 mutant embryos show the same SC overproliferation phenotype at 48 hpf

Similarly, we observed the same phenotype in mutant cd59uva47 embryos at 48 hpf (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B), demonstrating that mutation of cd59 was responsible for this phenotype

claim: Cd59 functions to limit overproliferation of SCs during development

source: Consistent with this finding, in vivo, time-lapse imaging of sox10:tagrfp-positive SCs along the pLLN showed cd59uva48 mutant SCs undergoing significantly more mitotic events than their wildtype siblings, with most of the increased cell divisions occurring between 48 and 55 hpf (Figure 4H, Videos 1 and 2)

claim: The number of SC divisions is similar between wildtype and cd59uva48 mutant larvae between 54 and 75 hpf

claim: cd59uva48 mutant larvae are capable of terminating SC proliferation at the same developmental stage as wildtype larvae

claim: cd59 mutation does not perturb SC death

claim: Neuronal proliferation is unaffected by cd59 mutation

claim: There is no difference in the number of migrating spinal motor nerve NCCs between wildtype and cd59uva48 mutant embryos

claim: Cd59 does not influence NCC proliferation

claim: There is no significant difference between the number of Sox10-positive cells along spinal motor nerves in wildtype and cd59uva48 larvae at 72 hpf

claim: Cd59 does not regulate proliferation of myelinating glia associated with the motor nerve

claim: There is no change in truncal neuromast number between wildtype and cd59uva48 mutant larvae at 7 dpf

claim: An increase in SC number does not alter neuromast formation

claim: cd59uva48 mutant SCs are capable of producing myelin

claim: There is no evidence of overlapping myelin sheaths in cd59uva48 mutant larvae at 7 dpf

claim: Axon volume is unaltered in cd59uva48 mutants

claim: Area of axon cross-sections is unaltered in cd59uva48 mutants
source: Because axon volume as well as area of axon cross-sections were unaltered, as indicated by acetylated α-Tubulin labeling (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and G) and TEM (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1I)
evidence: This is quantitative data from immunofluorescence and TEM shown in multiple figures

claim: There is a nonsignificant decrease in the average number of myelin wraps around each axon relative to the average area of the axon cross-section in cd59uva48 mutant larvae compared to wildtype siblings at 7 dpf
source: From these data, we observed a nonsignificant decrease in the average number of myelin wraps around each axon relative to the average area of the axon cross-section in cd59uva48 mutant larvae compared to wildtype siblings (Figure 5A and D)
evidence: This is quantitative data from TEM shown in Figure 5A and D

claim: The average axon area does not change between wildtype and cd59uva48 mutant nerves
source: Notably, the average axon area did not change between wildtype and mutant nerves (Figure 5A and D)
evidence: This is quantitative data from TEM shown in Figure 5A and D

claim: There is no change in the total number of myelinated axons between wildtype and cd59uva48 mutant nerves
source: nor was there a change in the total number of myelinated axons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H)
evidence: This is quantitative data from TEM shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H

claim: The decrease in myelinated nerve volume in cd59uva48 mutants could be related to a decrease in the number of myelin wraps on each axon
source: Therefore, although the decrease in myelin wrapping was not statistically significant, it indicates that the decrease in myelinated nerve volume observed in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and F could be related to a decrease in the number of myelin wraps on each axon
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the myelin wrapping and nerve volume data

claim: cd59uva48 mutant larvae have fewer discrete sodium channel clusters along the pLLN at 7 dpf
source: These studies revealed that cd59uva48 mutant larvae had fewer discrete sodium channel clusters along the pLLN (Figure 5B and E)
evidence: This is quantitative data from immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 5B and E

claim: cd59uva48 mutant nerves have fewer clusters of NF186 at 7 dpf
source: Accordingly, mutant nerves also had fewer clusters of NF186 (Figure 5C and F)
evidence: This is quantitative data from immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 5C and F

claim: NF186 and sodium channels always colocalize along the myelinated nerve in wildtype larvae
source: To confirm that our quantification was reliable, we co-labeled NF186 and sodium channels along mbpa:tagrfp-caax-positive nerves and observed that NF186 and sodium channels always colocalized along the myelinated nerve in wildtype larvae (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-labeling experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D

claim: Clusters of NF186 and sodium channels are bona fide nodes of Ranvier
source: indicating that these clusters of NF186 and sodium channels are bona fide nodes of Ranvier
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the colocalization data

claim: cd59uva48 mutant larvae do not form nodes of Ranvier normally
source: Considered together, these data indicate that cd59uva48 mutant larvae do not form nodes of Ranvier normally
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the node of Ranvier quantification data

claim: Cd59 is best known as a complement inhibitory protein
source: Outside of the nervous system, Cd59 is best known as a complement inhibitory protein
evidence: This is established knowledge about Cd59 function

claim: Complement is a molecular cascade within the innate immune system that aids in cell lysis of invading pathogens or aberrant cells
source: Complement is a molecular cascade within the innate immune system that aids in cell lysis of invading pathogens or aberrant cells in the body (Merle et al., 2015)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation

claim: Cd59 protects healthy cells from lytic death
source: This process lacks specificity and requires inhibitory proteins, such as Cd59, to protect healthy cells from lytic death (Davies et al., 1989)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation

claim: Cd59 binds to complement proteins 8 and 9 to prevent the polymerization of C9 and the formation of lytic pores
source: Cd59, specifically, acts at the end of the complement cascade where it binds to complement proteins 8 and 9 (C8 and C9, respectively) to prevent the polymerization of C9 and the subsequent formation of lytic pores (also known as membrane attack complexes [MACs] or terminal complement complexes [TCCs]) in healthy cell membranes (Meri et al., 1990; Ninomiya and Sims, 1992; Rollins et al., 1991)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations

claim: CD59a is neuroprotective in models of multiple sclerosis
source: This interaction is important throughout the adult body, including the nervous system, where CD59a is neuroprotective in models of multiple sclerosis (Mead et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citation

claim: CD59a is neuroprotective in models of neuromyelitis optica
source: and neuromyelitis optica (Yao and Verkman, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation

claim: Cd59 can facilitate vesicle signaling in insulin-producing pancreatic cells
source: Beyond complement-inhibitory functions, Cd59 can also facilitate vesicle signaling in insulin-producing pancreatic cells (Golec et al., 2019; Krus et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations

claim: Cd59 can suppress cell proliferation in T cells responding to a viral infection
source: suppress cell proliferation in T cells responding to a viral infection (Longhi et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citation

claim: Cd59 can suppress cell proliferation in smooth muscle cells in models of atherosclerosis
source: or smooth muscle cells in models of atherosclerosis (Li et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation

claim: Cd59 can orchestrate proximal-distal cell identity during limb regeneration
source: and orchestrate proximal-distal cell identity during limb regeneration (Echeverri and Tanaka, 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citation

claim: Patients with congenital CD59 deficiency present with polyneuropathies during infancy
source: Patients with CD59 dysfunction, such as those with congenital CD59 deficiency (Haliloglu et al., 2015; Höchsmann and Schrezenmeier, 2015; Karbian et al., 2018; Solmaz et al., 2020) or germline paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (Johnston et al., 2012), present with polyneuropathies during infancy
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations

claim: Patients with CD59 dysfunction continue to have nervous system dysfunction throughout their lives
source: and continue to have nervous system dysfunction throughout their lives
evidence: This is supported by the citations for CD59 deficiency patients

claim: Neurological symptoms in CD59 deficiency patients persist even with complement inhibition
source: Intriguingly, these neurological symptoms persist even with complement inhibition, the most common treatment for congenital CD59 deficiency (Höchsmann and Schrezenmeier, 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation

claim: CD59 has an additional role in the developing nervous system beyond complement inhibition
source: Together, these observations further indicate that CD59 has an additional role in the developing nervous system and requires further investigation
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the clinical observations

claim: cd59uva48 mutant larvae have more MACs localized to sox10:megfp-positive SC membranes compared to wildtype controls at 55 hpf
source: Using an antibody against C5b8-C5b9, which recognizes assembled MACs, we observed that cd59uva48 mutant larvae had more MACs localized to sox10:megfp-positive SC membranes compared to wildtype controls at 55 hpf (Figure 6A–C)
evidence: This is quantitative data from immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 6A–C

claim: Developing SCs are no longer protected from complement in cd59uva48 mutants
source: indicating that developing SCs are no longer protected from complement in cd59uva48 mutants
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MAC binding data

claim: Dexamethasone treatment in cd59uva48 mutant embryos restores SC numbers to wildtype levels
source: Excitingly, Dex treatment in cd59uva48 mutant embryos restored SC numbers to wildtype levels (Figure 7A and C)
evidence: This is quantitative data from dexamethasone treatment experiments shown in Figure 7A and C

claim: The number of SCs in wildtype larvae is significantly reduced by Dex treatment
source: Furthermore, when compared alone, the number of SCs in wildtype larvae was also significantly reduced by Dex treatment (Figure 7A and C)
evidence: This is quantitative data from dexamethasone treatment experiments shown in Figure 7A and C

claim: Developmental inflammation plays a role in homeostatic SC development
source: indicating that developmental inflammation plays a role in homeostatic SC development
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dexamethasone treatment data

claim: EdU incorporation in cd59uva48 mutant SCs returns to wildtype levels with Dex treatment from 24 to 55 hpf
source: In support of these findings, EdU incorporation in cd59uva48 mutant SCs from 48 to 55 hpf also returned to wildtype levels with Dex treatment from 24 to 55 hpf (Figure 7B and D)
evidence: This is quantitative data from EdU incorporation assays with dexamethasone treatment shown in Figure 7B and D

claim: Dex treatment suppresses SC proliferation
source: confirming that Dex treatment does suppress SC proliferation
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EdU incorporation data with dexamethasone treatment

claim: EdU incorporation in Dex-treated, wildtype SCs is reduced compared to DMSO-treated, wildtype controls
source: Interestingly, EdU incorporation in Dex-treated, wildtype SCs was also reduced compared to DMSO-treated, wildtype controls (Figure 7B and D)
evidence: This is quantitative data from EdU incorporation assays with dexamethasone treatment shown in Figure 7B and D

claim: Dex can alter homeostatic SC proliferation
source: showing that Dex can also alter homeostatic SC proliferation
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EdU incorporation data with dexamethasone treatment

claim: Developmental inflammation aids in normal SC proliferation
source: however, these data indicate that developmental inflammation aids in normal SC proliferation
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dexamethasone treatment experiments

claim: Developmental inflammation is amplified when cd59 is mutated
source: and that this process is amplified when cd59 is mutated
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dexamethasone treatment experiments

claim: Dex treatment dramatically increases the number of sodium channel clusters in cd59uva48 mutant larvae at 7 dpf
source: Remarkably, we observed that Dex treatment dramatically increased the number of sodium channel clusters in cd59uva48 mutant larvae, achieving cluster levels similar to wildtype siblings (Figure 8A and C)
evidence: This is quantitative data from immunofluorescence experiments with dexamethasone treatment shown in Figure 8A and C

claim: Dex treatment restores cd59uva48 mutant nerve volume to wildtype levels at 7 dpf
source: Similarly, when comparing myelinated nerve volume in mbpa:tagrfp-caax larvae at 7 dpf, we saw that Dex could also restore cd59uva48 mutant nerve volume to wildtype levels (Figure 8B and D)
evidence: This is quantitative data from confocal imaging with dexamethasone treatment shown in Figure 8B and D

claim: Inflammation-induced SC proliferation contributes to perturbed myelin and node of Ranvier development
source: Collectively, these data indicate that inflammation-induced SC proliferation contributes to perturbed myelin and node of Ranvier development
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dexamethasone treatment experiments

claim: Inhibition of developmental inflammation can protect nerve development after cd59 mutation
source: these experiments provide preliminary evidence that inhibition of developmental inflammation can protect nerve development after cd59 mutation
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dexamethasone treatment experiments

claim: Developmental inflammation stimulates SC proliferation and this process is balanced by Cd59 to ensure normal SC and myelinated nerve development
source: Overall, this data demonstrates that developmental inflammation stimulates SC proliferation and that this process is balanced by Cd59 to ensure normal SC and myelinated nerve development
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study drawn from all the experimental data
